q: What is the main idea of a function in this chapter?
options: A variable that keeps the result of a calculation for the rest of the program
A named block of code that can be run from many places, take values in and hand a value back
A separate file that holds one whole program and its data
A loop that repeats a block of code until its condition fails
why: The chapter gives a block of code a name so it can be run from many places, with values passed in and a value coming out.

q: Which keyword begins the statement that creates a new function?
options: func
def
define
function
why: Creating Functions introduces the def statement, which is followed by a call that runs the function.

q: When does the body of a function run?
options: Once, at the moment the def statement is executed, and never again
Every time any line of the program runs after the def statement
Each time the function is called, and not when the def statement is executed
Only the first time the function is called, then Python remembers the result
why: A def statement only creates the function and binds its name; the indented body executes when the function is called.

q: What does this program print?
code:
log = []
def hello():
    log.append('hi')
log.append('start')
hello()
hello()
print(log)
options: ['hi', 'start', 'hi', 'hi']
['start', 'hi', 'hi']
['start', 'hi']
['start']
why: The def statement does not run the body, so 'hi' is added only by the two calls after 'start'.

q: After the body of a called function ends, where does execution continue?
options: On the line after the call that started it
On the first line of the program again
On the last line of the program
On the first line of the function body again
why: Execution jumps into the body at a call and returns to the line after the call when the body ends.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def one():
    print('a', end=' ')
print('x', end=' ')
one()
print('y', end=' ')
one()
print('done')
options: x a a y done
x a y a done
a a x y done
x y a a done
why: Each call runs the body and then execution returns to the line after the call, so a appears between x, y and done.

q: Why does the chapter prefer one function to several pasted copies of the same code?
options: A fix is made in one place instead of in every pasted copy
Pasted copies make Python refuse to run the program
A function makes each line of code run faster than a pasted line
A function makes the printed output shorter than pasted code
why: Functions group code that runs more than once, so a change or a fix has to be made only once.

q: The same greeting block is pasted in three places and a typo is fixed in only two of them. What is the result?
options: Python notices the fix and updates the third copy for you
The program stops, because the three copies no longer match
The third copy still shows the old typo, which is the risk a single function removes
All three copies print the fixed text, because the code is identical
why: With pasted copies a fix has to be made in every place; a function keeps the code in one place so the copies cannot drift apart.

q: How does a value get into a function?
options: It is passed as an argument in the call and received by a parameter
It is written after the return keyword inside the body
It is found by Python from the names of the local variables
It is copied from the line after the call automatically
why: Arguments and parameters describe how values get into a function: the call passes them and the definition names the variables that receive them.

q: In  def say_hello_to(name):  called as  say_hello_to('Alice'),  which one is the argument?
options: name
'Alice'
say_hello_to
def
why: The value passed in the call is the argument; name is the parameter that receives it.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def show(name):
    name = name + '!'
    return name
name = 'Bo'
print(show('Al'), name)
options: Al! Al!
Al Bo!
Bo! Bo
Al! Bo
why: The parameter name is a separate variable that is forgotten when the function returns, so the global name stays 'Bo'.

q: What makes an argument a named parameter in a call?
options: It is always the last value in the call
It is identified by the name written before it, not by its position
It must be a text value put between quotation marks
It is identified by its type, not by its position
why: Python identifies most arguments by position but a named parameter by the name placed before it, like sep or end in print.

q: What does this program print?
code: print('a', 'b', sep='', end='!')
options: a b!
ab
a b
ab!
why: sep='' removes the space between the values and end='!' replaces the newline, so the output is ab!.

q: In  def f(a, /, b):  what does the slash mean?
options: The parameters before the slash can only be passed by name
The parameters after the slash cannot be used in the body
The value of a is divided by the value of b
The parameters before the slash can only be passed by position
why: Parameters before a slash in a definition can only be passed by position, and passing one by name raises a TypeError.

q: What does this program do?
options: ValueError
TypeError
NameError
why: w is before the slash so it cannot be passed by name, and w=3 in the call raises a TypeError.

q: Why is a keyword-only parameter useful in a function definition?
options: It lets the parameter keep its value between calls
It lets the parameter be left out even when it has no default
A call cannot pass it by position, so the call cannot be misread
It makes the function run faster than one with ordinary parameters
why: Parameters after a star must be passed by name, which turns a call that could be misread into a call that cannot.

q: What does this program print?
why: h is keyword-only with default 1: box(4, h=3) is 4 * 3 and box(5) uses the default, so 5 * 1.

q: When is the default value of a parameter evaluated?
options: Every time the function is called
Only when the caller leaves the argument out
Once, when the function is first called
Once, when the function is defined
why: A default value is evaluated once, when the function is defined, so one default object is shared by all the calls.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def add(x, box=[]):
    box.append(x)
    return box
add(1)
print(add(2))
why: The empty list default is created once and shared, so the second call appends to the list the first call already changed.

q: Why does a default of [] cause trouble while a default of 0 does not?
options: Python builds the list default again on every call but keeps the integer
The list is one shared object that can be changed in place, and an integer cannot be changed
A list is longer than an integer, so Python keeps it in memory
An integer is copied into each call, but a list is copied into none
why: A default is evaluated once, so a mutable default such as a list is shared between calls and accumulates the arguments.

q: Which change follows the tutorial's remedy for a function that keeps items in a list default?
options: Use an empty tuple as the default and call append on it later
Call the function once with a list before any other call
Use None as the default and create a new list inside when the parameter is None
Move the def statement to the end of the program
why: The remedy is a default of None that the function replaces with a new list on each call.

q: What does a function call evaluate to?
options: The name of the function that was called
The number of arguments in the call
Its return value, so the call can be used wherever a value can
The last line printed by the function body
why: Return values describe what a call evaluates to, which lets a call stand in for a value.

q: What does this program print?
options: double(3)
why: The inner call returns 6 and that value is the argument of the outer call, which returns 12.

q: Why can print(get_answer(3)) work when get_answer returns a value?
options: print runs the body of get_answer itself before printing
A function may only be called from inside a print call
The return value is printed by the return statement itself
A call is an expression, so its return value can be the argument of another call
why: The value a call evaluates to is its return value, and because a call is an expression it can be an argument to another call.

q: What does a return statement with no expression after it give back?
options: An empty string
The last value printed
None
why: If an expression list is present it is evaluated, else None is substituted, and control leaves the function.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def g():
    return 1
    print('after')
print(g())
options: after 1
after
None
why: return leaves the function with the value 1, so the print line after it never runs.

q: What does a function with no return statement give back?
options: An empty string
The value of its last line
None
why: Python adds return None to the end of a function with no return statement.

q: What does this program print?
options: None None
None 4
why: A bare return gives back None, so stop(-1) is None, and stop(4) returns 4.

q: A student writes  def add(a, b): a + b  and finds that print(add(1, 2)) shows None. Why?
options: The sum is computed but there is no return statement, so the call gives back None
The sum is stored in a and b, so nothing is left to show
print cannot show the value of a function call
Python only returns a value from functions with two parameters
why: Without a return statement Python adds return None, so the computed value is thrown away.

q: What does the value None stand for?
options: The number zero, written as a word
The absence of a value, and it is the only value of its own type
An empty string that has no characters
An error that stops the program at once
why: None stands for the absence of a value and is the only value of the NoneType data type.

q: How does PEP 8 say a value should be compared with None?
options: With == and != like any other value
With the len() function, since None has no length
With the type() function and the word None in quotes
With is or is not, not with the equality operators
why: PEP 8 says comparisons to singletons like None should always be done with is or is not.

q: What does this program print?
code:
result = print('a', end='|')
print(result)
options: a|
a|None
None
a|True
why: print returns None, so result holds None; the first print writes a| without a newline and the second prints None.

q: Which question does the call stack answer?
options: Which variables are global
How many arguments a call may have
Which exception matches an error
Where execution goes back to when a function returns
why: The Call Stack explains where execution goes when a function returns.

q: Why does Python remember the line that made a call?
options: So that execution can return there when the function ends
So that the line is run a second time before the body
So that the arguments can be printed later
So that the function can be called only from that line
why: Python remembers the line that called the function, so the call does not send execution one way to the top of the body.

q: Where are frame objects added to and removed from the call stack?
options: Only at the bottom
At either end, whichever is free
In the middle, next to the caller
Only at the top
why: Frame objects are added to and removed from the top of the call stack only, and the top frame is the function currently running.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def a():
    print('a1', end=' ')
    b()
    print('a2', end=' ')
def b():
    print('b', end=' ')
a()
options: b a1 a2
a1 b a2
a1 a2 b
a1 b
why: a() prints a1, waits while b() runs and prints b, then resumes and prints a2.

q: What happens when a function calls itself without ever stopping?
options: Python runs it forever without any message
Python crashes the computer by running out of memory
The interpreter stops it with a RecursionError
Python silently returns None after one call
why: The interpreter limits the depth of its stack and raises RecursionError instead of overflowing the C stack.

q: What does this program do?
options: None
RecursionError
SyntaxError
It runs forever
why: The function never stops calling itself, so the stack depth limit is reached and RecursionError is raised.

q: Why does  try: loop(0)  except RuntimeError:  catch the error of a function that calls itself forever?
options: RuntimeError is the name Python gives to every possible error
The except clause catches any error, whatever type is written
The try clause stops the recursion before the limit is reached
RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError, so the except clause matches
why: RecursionError is a subclass of RuntimeError, so an except clause naming RuntimeError matches it.

q: Which question do the scope topics answer?
options: How fast a function runs
How many times a function may be called
Which variable a name refers to
Which line called the function
why: Local and global scopes, the scope rules and the global statement say which variable a name refers to.

q: When is the scope of a function created and destroyed?
options: Created when the def statement runs and destroyed at the end of the program
Created when the program starts and destroyed when the function is called
Created when the program starts and destroyed when the def statement runs
Created when the function is called and destroyed when it returns
why: Scopes are containers created when a program starts or a function is called; a function's local scope is destroyed when the call returns.

q: What happens to a variable assigned inside a function when the function returns?
options: It is destroyed with the local scope of that call
It becomes a global variable with the same name
It is kept for the next call of the function
It is kept, but can be read only by other functions
why: A variable assigned inside a function exists in that call's local scope, which is destroyed when the function returns.

q: What does this program do?
code:
def spam():
    eggs = 99
spam()
print(eggs)
options: NameError
None
UnboundLocalError
why: eggs exists only in the local scope of spam(), which is gone after the call, so print(eggs) raises NameError.

q: Can code inside a function read a global variable that the function does not assign?
options: Yes, when there is no local variable of that name
No, a function can use only its own variables
Yes, but only after a global statement
No, unless the global variable is passed as an argument
why: There is one global scope and code in a local scope can read its variables when it has no local variable of that name.

q: What does this program print?
code:
limit = 3
def check(n):
    return n < limit
print(check(2), check(5))
options: True True
False False
True False
NameError
why: check() only reads limit, so it finds the global limit 3: 2 < 3 is True and 5 < 3 is False.

q: A global variable and a local variable in a function have the same name. How many variables are there?
options: Two, because each scope has its own variable
One, and the local assignment changes the global
One, and Python raises an error at the definition
Two, but the local one is deleted at once
why: The same name in different scopes gives different variables, which is why the book advises unique names.

q: What does this program print?
code:
x = 'global'
def f():
    x = 'local'
    return x
print(f(), x)
options: local local
global global
global local
local global
why: The x inside f is a separate local variable, so the global x still holds 'global'.

q: How many rules tell whether a name is local or global?
options: Two
Four
Three
Six
why: The chapter gives four rules for telling whether a name is local or global.

q: What does  global eggs  at the top of a function change?
options: It creates a new global variable that is empty
It makes eggs a constant that cannot be assigned
eggs in that function refers to the global variable, so assigning to it changes the global
It makes eggs local, but with the global value copied in
why: A global statement makes the name refer to the global variable, so assigning to it changes the global and no local variable is created.

q: What does this program print?
code:
count = 0
def bump():
    global count
    count += 1
bump()
bump()
print(count)
options: UnboundLocalError
why: Because of global count, each call changes the global variable, so it grows from 0 to 2.

q: A function only reads a name and never assigns it, and has no global statement. Is the name local or global?
options: Global
Local
Local, but only during the first call
Neither; Python raises an error
why: One a function only uses is global; only an assigned name is local.

q: What does this program print?
code:
a = 1
def f():
    return a
def g():
    a = 2
    return a
print(f(), g(), a)
why: f only reads a so it uses the global 1, g assigns a so its a is a local 2, and the global a is unchanged.

q: Why is a name local for the whole function even when the assignment comes after the first use?
options: The compiler scans the whole body for name-binding operations before the function runs
Python runs the function twice and compares the two runs
Python decides only when it reaches the first use of the name
Python asks the caller to say which variables are local
why: The compiler decides by scanning the whole function body for name-binding operations, not line by line as the code runs.

q: What does UnboundLocalError report?
options: A local variable was used before it was assigned a value
A global variable was deleted while the program ran
A function was called with too many arguments
A name was never written anywhere in the program
why: Using a local variable before assigning it raises UnboundLocalError, a subclass of NameError.

q: What does this program do?
options: UnboundLocalError
NameError
why: The assignment n = 2 makes n local for the whole function even though it never runs, so the read of n fails with UnboundLocalError.

q: UnboundLocalError is a subclass of which error?
options: TypeError
NameError
ValueError
RuntimeError
why: The definition states that UnboundLocalError is a subclass of NameError.

q: Which wording does Python 3.14 use in the message of this error?
options: local variable 'eggs' referenced before assignment
cannot access local variable 'eggs' where it is not associated with a value
name 'eggs' is not defined anywhere in the program
eggs was used before def, so it has no value
why: In 3.14 the message reads cannot access local variable where it is not associated with a value, while the chapter shows the older wording.

q: What does a nonlocal statement let an inner function do?
options: Rebind a name of the global scope
Delete a name of the enclosing function
Read a name of the caller of the function
Rebind a name of the enclosing function
why: The nonlocal statement makes the listed names refer to names bound in the nearest enclosing function, so an inner function can rebind them.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def outer():
    n = 0
    def inner():
        nonlocal n
        n += 1
    inner()
    inner()
    return n
print(outer())
options: UnboundLocalError
why: nonlocal n makes inner() rebind the n of outer(), so two calls raise it from 0 to 2.

q: What does exception handling change about an error in a program?
options: It turns a crash into something the program can recover from
It stops the error from ever being raised
It makes the error message shorter
It turns the error into a warning that is never shown
why: Exception handling turns an error from a crash into something a program can recover from.

q: Which statements decide what happens after an error raises an exception?
options: if and else
def and return
try and except
for and while
why: An error raises an exception, and try and except statements decide what happens next.

q: What happens to the rest of a try clause after one of its lines raises a matching exception?
options: It still runs, and then the except clause runs
It is skipped and the program ends after the except clause
It runs again from the first line of the try clause
It is skipped, the except clause runs, and execution continues after the try statement
why: When an exception occurs the rest of the try clause is skipped and, if the type matches, the except clause runs.

q: What does this program print?
code:
try:
    print('a', end=' ')
    x = 1 / 0
    print('b', end=' ')
except ZeroDivisionError:
    print('c', end=' ')
print('d')
options: a b d
a b c d
a c
a c d
why: The division raises ZeroDivisionError, so b is skipped, the except clause prints c, and execution continues with d.

q: A function called from a try clause raises an error. Which clause handles it?
options: Nothing; the error ends the program inside the function
The except clause, after which the try clause continues
The except clause of the try statement, and execution does not return into the try clause
The function's caller, after the program is restarted
why: An error inside a function called from a try clause is caught by that clause, and execution does not return to the try clause.

q: What does this program print?
options: spam 2 21.0 spam 0 err spam 1 42.0
spam 2 21.0 spam 0 err
spam 2 21.0 err
spam 0 err
why: The second call divides by zero inside spam(), execution jumps to the except clause, and the third call is never made.

q: Since Python 3.14, which except clause is allowed when there is no as clause?
options: except TimeoutError, ConnectionRefusedError:
except TimeoutError and ConnectionRefusedError:
except TimeoutError + ConnectionRefusedError:
except TimeoutError or ConnectionRefusedError:
why: From 3.14 an except clause can list several exception types without brackets when it has no as clause.

q: A clause must list two exception types and also use as. What does Python 3.14 require?
options: The types must be in brackets
Nothing; the unbracketed form works with as
The as name must come before the types
Only one exception type may be listed
why: 3.14 rejects the unbracketed form with as unless the types are in brackets.

q: What is the point of the modern-practice topics next to the chapter's functions?
options: They add what current Python offers around functions
They replace the functions the chapter teaches
They list features that older Python versions require
They show how to write functions without def
why: An advanced course pairs the chapter's functions with what current Python adds around them.

q: Which function header carries annotations on a parameter and on the result?
options: def area(w: int, h: int) -> int:
def area(w = int, h = int) -> int:
def area(int w, int h): int
def area(w, h) = int:
why: Annotations on a function's parameters and result are written with a colon after a parameter and an arrow before the final colon.

q: In Python 3.14, what happens when  def f(x: Undefined): return x  is defined and then f(1) is called?
options: NameError is raised at the def statement
f(1) works, because the annotation is not evaluated at definition
NameError is raised when f is called
SyntaxError is raised because Undefined is unknown
why: Since 3.14 annotations are evaluated only when necessary, so names that do not exist yet can be used.

q: In Python 3.14, f is defined with an annotation of a name that does not exist yet. What happens when f.__annotations__ is read?
options: The annotation is silently dropped
None is returned for that annotation
NameError is raised until the name exists
The name is created automatically
why: Annotations are looked up only on request, so reading them raises NameError until the names exist.

q: According to the style topic, what matters besides how a function is written?
options: How many lines the function has
How the function is meant to be used
How many functions the program defines
Which version of Python it was written in
why: How a function is meant to be used matters as much as how it is written.

q: What does it mean to treat a function as a black box?
options: Only its parameters and its return value matter, and its local variables affect nothing else
Its code is hidden by Python and cannot be read
Its variables are shared with all the other functions
It may only be called once in the program
why: A function can be treated as a black box: inputs go in, the return value comes out, and its local variables do not affect other functions.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def sq(n):
    tmp = n * n
    return tmp
tmp = 'mine'
sq(5)
print(tmp)
options: None
mine
NameError
why: The tmp inside sq is local to that call, so the global tmp is not affected.

q: Which lines belong to the body of a function?
options: Every line of the file that comes after the def line
The indented lines under the def line
Only the first line after the colon of the def line
The lines up to the first blank line below the def line
why: The indentation under the def line marks the body, and the first line back at the left margin is no longer part of it.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def f():
    x = 1
    return x
    x = 2
print(f())
options: None
(no output)
why: The call ends at the return statement, so the assignment x = 2 after it is part of the body but never runs.

q: What does the name hello refer to after the statement def hello(): pass has run?
options: The text of the function body, stored as a string
The value None, which the body returns when it is called
A copy of the body that is made again at every call
A function object that the def statement created
why: A def statement builds a function object and binds the name to it; the name is only a label for that object.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def hello():
    return 'hi'
same = hello
print(same is hello, same())
options: False hi
True None
True hi
hi hi
why: same = hello gives the second name to the same function object, so same is hello is True and same() runs the body that returns 'hi'.

q: Why does the line def = 3 stop a program with a SyntaxError?
options: def is the name of a built-in function, and built-in names cannot be given a new value
An assignment may not use a number on its right side
def can only be written inside a function body
def is a keyword with a fixed meaning, so it cannot be a variable name
why: Keywords such as def, return and global are reserved by the language and cannot be used as names.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import keyword
print(keyword.iskeyword('print'), keyword.iskeyword('def'))
options: True True
False True
False False
True False
why: keyword.iskeyword is False for print, which is an ordinary built-in function, and True for def, which is reserved.

q: What can the body of a lambda expression contain?
options: A single expression, whose value the function returns
Any number of statements, indented under the word lambda
Only a return statement that names the value
A def statement that gives the function its name
why: A lambda is limited to one expression; statements, including return, are not allowed in it.

q: What does this program print?
code:
f = lambda a, b: a * b + 1
print(f(2, 3), f.__name__)
options: 7 f
6 <lambda>
7 <lambda>
7 lambda
why: f(2, 3) is 2 * 3 + 1, which is 7, and a function made by a lambda expression keeps the generic name <lambda>.

q: Where can the name inner be used when a def statement for it sits inside the body of outer?
options: Anywhere in the program after outer has been defined
Only in the line directly after the def inner line
In any function that outer calls, but not in outer itself
Inside outer, while a call of outer is running
why: The inner def binds its name in the local scope of outer, so the name exists only during a call of outer.

q: What does this program print?
options: NameError
in!
None
TypeError
why: inner is local to outer, so the name is not defined at the top level where the program uses it.

q: What must a program do before it can call random.randint?
options: Define a function named random at the top of the file
Import the module random with an import statement
Assign the number 0 to a variable called random
Call input() so that Python loads the library
why: The dotted name looks up randint inside the module, and the name random exists only after the import statement.

q: What does this program print?
code:
import random
print(random.randint(4, 4))
options: (no output)
why: random.randint(a, b) returns an integer from a to b including both ends, so with a and b equal the result is always that number.

q: What does this program do?
code: print(random.randint(1, 3))
options: It prints a number from 1 to 3
It prints None
NameError
ValueError
why: Without the import line the name random is not defined, so the first line stops with NameError.

q: How does Python match the arguments in divmod(17, 5) to the parameters of divmod?
options: By size: the larger value always goes to the first parameter
By name: Python uses the variable names of the caller
By type: integers are matched before strings and floats
By position: the first argument goes to the first parameter
why: A positional argument is matched to a parameter by its place in the call.

q: What does this program print?
code: print(divmod(17, 5), divmod(5, 17))
why: divmod gives the quotient and remainder of the first number divided by the second, so swapping the arguments changes the result.

q: Why can the call get_answer(r) be written directly inside print( )?
options: Python prints the function's code when it sees the call
The call evaluates to its return value, which print receives
print runs get_answer after it has printed the empty line
A call is a statement, and Python allows statements to be nested inside the parentheses of other calls
why: A call is an expression: it is replaced by the value the function returns, and that value is passed to the outer call.

q: What does this program print?
why: The inner call double(3) gives 6, the outer call gives 12, and adding 1 gives 13.

q: Which test does PEP 8 recommend for finding out whether the variable spam holds None?
options: spam == None
not spam
spam = None
spam is None
why: Comparisons to singletons such as None should be made with is or is not, not with the equality operators.

q: What does this program print?
options: none none
value none
value value
none value
why: The test x is None is True only for None itself, so the argument 0 still counts as a given value.

q: What does the frame object of a function call let Python do when the call ends?
options: Restore the values that the global variables had when the function was called
Start the function again from its first line
Return to the line of the code that made the call
Delete the function so it cannot be called again
why: A frame object stores where the call came from, so execution can continue there when the function returns.

q: What does this program print?
options: inner
<module>
outer
f_back
why: currentframe() is the frame of inner, its f_back is the frame of the caller, and the code name of that frame is outer.

q: What does a recursive function need so that the chain of calls ends?
options: A global variable that counts the calls and stops the chain when it reaches the limit
A try statement around every recursive call
A second parameter with a default value
A base case that returns without calling itself
why: Without a branch that returns directly, every call makes another call and the stack grows until RecursionError.

q: What does this program print?
options: RecursionError
why: f(4) is 4 * f(3), which unfolds to 4 * 3 * 2 * 1, and the base case n <= 1 returns 1.

q: After its own local scope, where does Python look for a name used inside a nested function?
options: In the scope of the function that contains it
In the built-in scope, before anything else
In the scope of the function that called it
Nowhere; the name must be passed as a parameter
why: The lookup goes from the local scope outwards through the enclosing functions, then global, then built-in.

q: What does this program print?
options: NameError
UnboundLocalError
why: inner only reads n, so it finds the n of outer in the enclosing scope and returns 5 + 1.

q: Why does print work in a program that never defined it?
options: Python adds a def print() statement to the top of every file it reads before running it
print is a keyword, and keywords need no definition
Its name is found in the built-in scope, the last place searched
The global scope is copied from the previous program
why: Names such as print and len live in the builtins namespace, which is searched after the global scope.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def f():
    len = 10
    return len
print(f(), len('abc'))
why: len = 10 inside f creates a local variable and leaves the built-in len alone, so len('abc') still gives 3.

q: What does the rule of local isolation say about the variables of one function?
options: They stay available to the whole program after the call
Code in another function cannot use them
They can be read but not changed by other functions
They are copied into the global scope when the call ends
why: Code in one function's local scope cannot use the variables in any other local scope.

q: What does this program print?
code:
def spam():
    eggs = 'spam'
    bacon()
    return eggs
def bacon():
    eggs = 'bacon'
print(spam())
options: spam
bacon
None
NameError
why: bacon assigns its own eggs, which is a different variable from the eggs of spam, so spam still returns 'spam'.

q: Which function can use a global variable without a global statement?
options: Only one that is defined before the variable is created
Only one that has no parameters at all
One that assigns the name once on its last line
One that only reads the name and never assigns it
why: If a function only uses a name and never assigns it, Python takes it to be the global variable.

q: What does this program print?
code:
limit = 3
def over(n):
    return n > limit
print(over(5), over(2))
options: False False
True False
True True
False True
why: over() only reads limit, so it uses the global value 3: 5 is greater than 3 and 2 is not.

q: In which order does Python search the scopes for a name used inside a nested function?
options: Global, local, enclosing functions, built-in
Built-in, global, enclosing functions, local
Local, enclosing functions, global, built-in
Enclosing functions, local, built-in, global
why: The name is resolved in the nearest scope that has it, starting from the local scope and moving outwards.

q: What does this program print?
options: g g
e g
e e
g e
why: inner has no x of its own, so the nearest x is the one in outer; the global x is a different variable and stays 'g'.

q: Which mistake raises a NameError?
options: Using a name that none of the scopes contains
Dividing a number by zero
Calling a function with one argument too many
Passing a text that is not a number to int()
why: NameError means that the name is not defined in any scope that the line can see.

q: What does this program do?
code:
def f():
    y = 1
f()
print(y)
options: It prints 1
It prints None
NameError
UnboundLocalError
why: y is created in the local scope of f and is destroyed when the call returns, so the top level cannot see it.

q: When does Python decide which names in a function are local?
options: When each name is used for the first time while the call is running, line by line
When the function is called with its arguments
When the function returns its value to the caller
Before the function runs, by scanning its whole body for assignments
why: The compiler builds the symbol table from the text of the function, so the decision does not depend on which lines run.

q: In the function f, x = 'local' sits under if False. Why is the line return x an error, not a use of the global x?
options: Python runs the if block once to check the assignment and then discards its effect
The global x is deleted when the function is defined
A function may not return a variable of the same name as a global
The assignment makes x local in the whole body, and that local has no value
why: The symbol table marks x as local for the entire body, so the global x is never consulted.

q: What does the name e hold in the clause except ZeroDivisionError as e:?
options: The text of the line that failed
The exception object that was raised
The number by which the program divided
The name of the function that was running
why: The as clause binds the exception instance, whose args and text describe the error.

q: What does this program print?
options: division by zero
ZeroDivisionError
('division by zero',)
why: e.args is the tuple of arguments the exception was created with, here the single message string.

q: In a traceback, which line says what kind of error happened?
options: The first line, Traceback (most recent call last):
The line with the file name closest to the top
The last line, with the exception type and its message
The source line printed above the message
why: The last line names the exception; the lines above it show the calls that led to it.

q: A traceback lists a call in <module> and below it a call in spam. What does that order show?
options: spam was defined after the main program ran, so Python lists it last by the time of definition
The main program was called by spam
spam was called from the main program and the error happened inside spam
The error happened in the main program, not in spam
why: The most recent call comes last, so the frames are listed from the main program down to where the error was raised.

q: Which exception does the expression 7 % 0 raise?
options: ZeroDivisionError
OverflowError
ValueError
TypeError
why: Division, floor division and modulo with a zero second operand all raise ZeroDivisionError.

q: What does this program print?

ZeroDivisionError
why: 6 / 3 is 2.0; the division by zero is caught inside safe, which then returns 0.

q: Why does the clause except Exception not catch a KeyboardInterrupt?
options: Ctrl-C is handled by the operating system, not Python
KeyboardInterrupt is not a subclass of Exception
An except clause never catches an error from a keypress
KeyboardInterrupt can only be caught inside a function
why: KeyboardInterrupt inherits from BaseException, so a handler for Exception does not match it.

q: What does this program print?
options: zero
arith zero
ZeroDivisionError
arith
why: The first matching clause runs, and ZeroDivisionError is a subclass of ArithmeticError, so the broad clause wins.

q: Which tools do the chapter's short programs bring in that the chapter had not covered yet?
options: recursion, nonlocal and lambda
global, return and def
time.sleep, KeyboardInterrupt and sys.exit
annotations, comments and naming

So that a division by zero cannot happen in the loop
So that the loop runs more slowly, which makes the animation easier to watch on screen
So that the program can be run only once
why: The loop never ends by itself, and the except clause for KeyboardInterrupt calls sys.exit to stop it cleanly.

q: What does the variable indent_increasing decide in the zigzag program?

How long the program pauses between two lines
Whether indent grows or shrinks on the next pass of the loop
Whether the program stops after the next pass

The rising half and the falling half of one spike
One line of dashes and then its mirror image
The same triangle twice, at two speeds

q: What does the call time.sleep(0.1) do?

Ends the program after a tenth of a second
Repeats the next line ten times
Prints the current time with one decimal
why: The function suspends execution for the given number of seconds, which may be a fraction.

q: Which keypress makes Python raise KeyboardInterrupt in a running program?

Esc
Ctrl-D
Ctrl-C

q: What does sys.exit() do when nothing catches the exception it raises?
options: Restarts the program from the first line
Ends the program with an exit status
Prints the traceback and continues
Closes only the function that called it

q: What does Python do with the annotation int in def f(a: int)?

Converts every argument to an integer
Raises a TypeError at the call whenever an argument is not an integer, to protect the function

At the next semicolon on the same line
At the next blank line in the file
At the closing parenthesis of the statement
